international.canonicalTopic: India rejects Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling on Indus Waters Treaty
international.headline: India rejects Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling on Indus Waters Treaty
facts: India rejected the Permanent Court of Arbitration’s ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty, asserting that the tribunal lacks authority over India’s sovereign decisions; India did not participate in the proceedings and does not recognise the tribunal’s legitimacy.

India placed the treaty in abeyance on 2025-04-23 after the Pahalgam terror attack of 2025-04-22; it said the treaty would remain in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably ends support for cross-border terrorism.
The Indus Waters Treaty was signed by India and Pakistan on 1960-09-19 in Karachi and brokered by the World Bank; Jawaharlal Nehru represented India and Ayub Khan represented Pakistan.
Ravi, Beas and Sutlej are the eastern rivers allocated mainly for India’s use; Indus, Jhelum and Chenab are the western rivers allocated mainly to Pakistan, subject to certain Indian usage rights.
The Permanent Court of Arbitration was established in 1899 and is based at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands; it is distinct from the International Court of Justice.
The Indus originates on the Tibetan Plateau, passes through China/Tibet, India and Pakistan, and drains into the Arabian Sea.
international.summary: India disputed the tribunal’s authority in a ruling concerning the Indus Waters Treaty and reiterated that the treaty remains in abeyance. The disagreement raises questions about treaty interpretation, water-sharing and regional security.
international.staticLink: The treaty divides the Indus basin rivers into eastern and western groups, with specified allocations and usage rights.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The Indus Waters Treaty was brokered by the World Bank; the Permanent Court of Arbitration is headquartered at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
international.mainsAngle: Examine the relationship between transboundary water governance, treaty obligations and national security in South Asia.

international.canonicalTopic: Visegrád Group supports India’s permanent membership in the UNSC
international.headline: Visegrád Group members back India’s candidature for permanent UNSC membership
facts: At the first Foreign Ministers’ Meeting between India and the Visegrád Group, all four member countries supported India’s candidature for permanent membership of the United Nations Security Council.
The Visegrád Group was formed in 1991. Its members are the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia.
The grouping was formed after leaders of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary met at Visegrád, Hungary; it became a four-member group after Czechoslovakia split in 1993.
The UNSC has 15 members: five permanent members—China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States—and ten non-permanent members serving two-year terms.
international.summary: The four Visegrád Group countries expressed support for India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council at their first Foreign Ministers’ meeting with India.
international.staticLink: The UN Security Council has 15 members and is responsible for maintaining international peace and security.
international.prelimsTakeaway: Visegrád Group members: Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia; the UNSC has five permanent and ten non-permanent members.
international.mainsAngle: Discuss the case for reforming the UN Security Council and the significance of international support for India’s candidature.

international.canonicalTopic: India–Russia bilateral trade target for 2030
international.headline: India and Russia set USD 100 billion annual trade target for 2030
facts: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks in New Delhi and agreed on an annual bilateral trade target of USD 100 billion by 2030.
They discussed cooperation in key sectors and establishing a new investment platform; Putin invited Modi to Russia for the next annual India–Russia Summit.

Bilateral trade in 2025–26 was approximately USD 60 billion; India’s imports from Russia were USD 55.36 billion and exports were USD 4.49 billion, producing a trade deficit of approximately USD 50.87 billion.
The India–Russia Strategic Partnership dates to 2000; it became a Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership in 2010.
international.summary: India and Russia agreed to pursue a USD 100 billion annual trade target by 2030 and discussed investment and sectoral cooperation. The notes report a substantial bilateral trade deficit for 2025–26.
international.staticLink: Defence, energy, nuclear power, space, trade and investment are identified as major areas of India–Russia cooperation.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The agreed annual trade target is USD 100 billion by 2030; the notes give 2025–26 trade at approximately USD 60 billion.
international.mainsAngle: Evaluate the opportunities and challenges in expanding India–Russia trade, including trade-balance concerns and diversification of cooperation.

international.canonicalTopic: India–Japan Year of Shared Horizons 2027
international.headline: 2027 to be observed as the India–Japan Year of Shared Horizons
facts: India and Japan designated 2027 as the India–Japan Year of Shared Horizons to mark 75 years of diplomatic relations, which began in 1952.
The celebrations are to begin with a friendly cricket match during the Aichi–Nagoya Asian Games 2026.

MAGE-75 is intended to promote partnerships in manga, anime, gaming and immersive creative technologies; Shared Future-75 will bring together youth, professionals and academics for policy ideas; RASA-75 (Rang, Sur and Sakura) will showcase Indian and Japanese arts and heritage.
The two countries’ Special Strategic and Global Partnership dates from 2014.
international.summary: The year-long observance will mark 75 years of India–Japan diplomatic relations and feature creative-industry, policy and cultural initiatives.

international.mainsAngle: Explain how cultural, youth and technology initiatives can complement India–Japan strategic and economic cooperation.

international.canonicalTopic: Larak Island and the Strait of Hormuz
international.headline: Larak Island’s strategic position near the Strait of Hormuz
facts: Larak is an Iranian island near Bandar Abbas, east of Qeshm Island and south of Hormuz Island.
Its position near the Strait of Hormuz gives it relevance for maritime surveillance and coastal defence and allows monitoring of crude oil and LNG shipments.
The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman; Iran lies to its north and the Oman/UAE region to its south.
international.summary: The notes highlight Larak Island’s location beside the Strait of Hormuz and the strategic importance of the nearby maritime route for energy shipping.
international.staticLink: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
international.prelimsTakeaway: Larak Island lies near Bandar Abbas, east of Qeshm Island and south of Hormuz Island.
international.mainsAngle: Explain how maritime chokepoints influence energy security, trade flows and regional strategic calculations.

international.canonicalTopic: Houthi capture of Mayun Island in Yemen
international.headline: Houthis capture strategic Mayun Island in Yemen
facts: The Houthis captured Mayun Island, about 3.5 km off Yemen’s western coast, after Yemeni government forces withdrew.
The notes link the capture to efforts to gain greater control over the maritime route through Bab el-Mandeb; they also report the capture of Mocha port city and a Saudi airstrike on its airport.
Bab el-Mandeb lies between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea and links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea.
international.summary: The reported capture of Mayun Island drew attention to Bab el-Mandeb, a key maritime passage for global energy and commercial shipping.
international.staticLink: Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, opening to the Arabian Sea.
international.prelimsTakeaway: Mayun Island is about 3.5 km off Yemen’s western coast; Bab el-Mandeb lies between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea.
international.mainsAngle: Analyse the vulnerability of global trade and energy routes to instability around maritime chokepoints.

international.canonicalTopic: G20 Energy Ministers’ Meeting consensus outcomes
international.headline: India joins G20 energy consensus on access, infrastructure, water reuse and critical minerals
facts: At a three-day G20 Energy Ministers’ Meeting in Houston, Texas, under the US G20 Presidency, India and other member countries adopted four consensus outcome statements.
The four areas were household energy access, infrastructure regulatory capacity, voluntary water reuse, and resilient critical-mineral value chains.
The stated goals include strengthening energy security, infrastructure, water-resource resilience and critical-mineral supply chains.

The G20 was established in 1999; its membership comprises 19 countries, the European Union and the African Union. The African Union became a permanent member in 2023; India held the presidency in 2023.

international.canonicalTopic: UN General Assembly declaration on sea-level rise
international.headline: UN General Assembly adopts declaration on sea-level rise
facts: The 81st United Nations General Assembly unanimously adopted a declaration addressing risks to low-lying coastal countries and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) from sea-level rise.
The declaration seeks principles to safeguard statehood continuity, permanent maritime rights and human rights if territory is submerged because of climate change.
The process originated under UN General Assembly Decision 78/558; Australia and Cabo Verde were co-facilitators.
It calls for greater climate adaptation and loss-and-damage finance, and protection for displaced populations and cultural identities.
The UN General Assembly has 193 members and is headquartered in New York.
international.summary: The declaration addresses legal and human-rights challenges for states and communities threatened by rising seas, alongside calls for adaptation and climate finance.
international.staticLink: UN General Assembly; Small Island Developing States; climate adaptation and loss-and-damage finance.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The UN General Assembly has 193 members; the sea-level-rise declaration process was initiated under Decision 78/558 with Australia and Cabo Verde as co-facilitators.
international.mainsAngle: Consider how sea-level rise challenges sovereignty, maritime entitlements, state continuity and the protection of displaced communities.

international.canonicalTopic: India at the 70th International Whaling Commission meeting
international.headline: India reaffirms cetacean conservation commitment at IWC meeting
facts: India reaffirmed its commitment to science-based cetacean conservation at the 70th meeting of the International Whaling Commission in Hobart, Australia.
The IWC is the principal intergovernmental body concerned with whale conservation and whaling regulation; its work also covers dolphins and porpoises.
The IWC was established under the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling, signed in Washington on December 2, 1946.
The IWC secretariat is in Impington, Cambridge, United Kingdom; the commercial whaling moratorium has been in place since 1986.
international.summary: India reiterated a science-based conservation approach at the IWC meeting, whose remit covers whales and other cetaceans.
international.staticLink: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling; cetaceans; commercial whaling moratorium.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The IWC was established in 1946; its commercial whaling moratorium dates from 1986 and its secretariat is in Impington, Cambridge.
international.mainsAngle: Examine how intergovernmental conservation bodies balance species protection and regulation of human activities.

international.canonicalTopic: OneSCD Global Partnership for sickle cell disease
international.headline: OneSCD Global Partnership launched to strengthen sickle cell care
facts: India co-hosted the launch of the OneSCD Global Partnership during the 81st UN General Assembly in New York.

The partnership aims to advance health equity and improve sickle cell disease care by strengthening national programmes and expanding approaches across prevention, diagnosis, treatment and continuing care.

Nigeria hosted the initiative; co-conveners included UNICEF, the World Health Organization, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, Global Sickle Cell Disease Coalition and St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital.
Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder in which red blood cells become sickle-shaped and can affect blood flow and oxygen supply.

India’s National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission was launched in 2023 and targets eliminating sickle cell anaemia as a public-health problem by 2047 through screening, prevention, counselling and disease management.
international.summary: The partnership seeks to improve sickle cell disease care and health equity through stronger national programmes and wider access to prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

international.prelimsTakeaway: OneSCD was launched during the 81st UN General Assembly; India’s national mission, launched in 2023, has a 2047 elimination target.
international.mainsAngle: Discuss how screening, counselling and coordinated health systems can reduce the disease burden and improve equity in access to care.

international.canonicalTopic: US support for the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor
international.headline: US backs IMEC as a potential energy-security route
facts: US President Donald Trump announced support for the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor amid energy-supply disruptions in West Asia and the Strait of Hormuz.
At a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council and Arab-country leaders, Trump said the corridor could reduce dependence on energy routes vulnerable to Iran-related disruptions.
The corridor was announced at the New Delhi G20 Summit in September 2023.
Its eastern corridor links India with the Arabian Gulf and its northern corridor links the Arabian Gulf with Europe.

Planned components include railways, maritime transport, electricity and digital connectivity, and clean-hydrogen infrastructure; its stated objective is improved connectivity, trade and economic integration.
international.summary: US support for IMEC was presented in the context of energy security and alternative connectivity routes linking India, West Asia and Europe.
international.staticLink: India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor; New Delhi G20 Summit 2023; energy security and multimodal connectivity.
international.prelimsTakeaway: IMEC was announced in September 2023; its eastern corridor is India–Arabian Gulf and its northern corridor is Arabian Gulf–Europe.
international.mainsAngle: Evaluate IMEC’s potential contribution to connectivity, trade diversification and energy security, while considering implementation challenges.

international.canonicalTopic: Proposal for Canada to become an EU associate member
international.headline: European Commission proposes an associate-member pathway for Canada
facts: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed a route for Canada to become the European Union’s first “Associate Member” as part of an “Alliance for the Future.”
The proposal seeks closer Canada–EU links in defence procurement, critical supply chains and technology partnerships.
The proposed status would not amount to full EU membership and would not automatically confer institutional voting rights or full access to the EU Single Market.
The notes state that this is only a proposed concept and that no associate-membership category exists under the EU’s founding treaties.
The European Union has 27 members and is headquartered in Brussels; 21 member states use the euro.
international.summary: The proposal envisages a new form of Canada–EU association, but it remains a concept rather than an established membership category.
international.staticLink: European Union; Maastricht Treaty; distinctions between EU membership and proposed association arrangements.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The EU has 27 member states and is headquartered in Brussels; the proposed associate status is not full membership and has not been established in the founding treaties.
international.mainsAngle: Consider how new forms of external partnership could deepen strategic cooperation without extending full membership rights.

international.canonicalTopic: Italy's restrictions on full-face coverings in schools
international.headline: Italy bans burqas and niqabs in schools
facts: The Italian government under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni banned full-face coverings, including burqas and niqabs, in schools; the notes say the hijab is not prohibited because it leaves the face visible.
The stated penalties range from €200 to €1,000; where minors breach the rule, fines are imposed on parents.
Some foreign students without adequate Italian proficiency are limited to 30% of first-year classes, with different criteria for primary and secondary schools.
The government said the measures seek linguistic integration, avoid excessive concentration of students and promote equal educational opportunity.
international.summary: Italy introduced school rules restricting full-face coverings and limiting the share of some first-year classes for students lacking sufficient Italian proficiency.
international.staticLink: Freedom of religion; equality and integration in public education.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The measure described covers burqas and niqabs, not the face-visible hijab; the stated fine range is €200–€1,000.

international.canonicalTopic: United Russia result in State Duma elections
international.headline: United Russia wins 355 seats in State Duma elections
facts: Russia’s Central Election Commission reported that United Russia won 355 of the State Duma’s 450 seats.
The party secured 57.83% of the party-list vote, compared with 49.8% in 2021, and exceeded its previous 343-seat record from 2016.
The result gave United Russia a constitutional majority, according to the notes.
Voter turnout was approximately 59.3%; the notes describe these as the first State Duma elections since the start of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022.
The State Duma is the lower house of Russia’s Federal Assembly; its term is five years and the upper house is the Federation Council.

facts: India-born author Salman Rushdie was selected for the US National Book Foundation’s Lifetime Achievement Award; the presentation is scheduled for November 18, 2026, in Manhattan, New York.
Rushdie is to become the award’s 39th recipient and its fourth recipient born outside the United States.

The National Book Foundation was established in 1989 and is headquartered in New York City; it administers the National Book Awards and promotes literature in the United States.

international.canonicalTopic: UNESCO International Literacy Prizes 2026
international.headline: UNESCO presents 2026 International Literacy Prizes in Mexico
facts: UNESCO presented the 2026 International Literacy Prizes during the International Literacy Day celebration in Chiapas, Mexico, under the theme “Literacy for people, the planet and prosperity.”
Each laureate receives USD 30,000, a medal and a diploma; the prizes recognise effective and innovative work in basic and functional literacy.
The King Sejong Literacy Prize winners listed were Rutu Foundation (Netherlands), WAER Waters Charity Foundation (Nigeria) and BibloRed (Colombia).
The Confucius Prize winners listed were Alsama Project (Lebanon), Government of Chiapas (Mexico) and Hat Yai City Municipality (Thailand).

The Rutu Foundation’s Language Friendly School works across around 70 schools in 12 countries; WAER Waters Charity Foundation’s Project PAL offers solar-powered literacy centres for out-of-school children.

The Government of Chiapas’s Chiapas Puede provides bilingual Spanish–Indigenous language instruction across 121 municipalities; Hat Yai’s Language for Life combines multilingual literacy with disaster communication, climate awareness and community resilience.

International Literacy Day was proclaimed in 1966; the prizes were established in 1967. The King Sejong Prize was established in 1989 with support from the Republic of Korea, and the Confucius Prize in 2005 with support from China.
The prizes support literacy and numeracy goals including SDG 4.6.

international.canonicalTopic: UN General Assembly equal-area world maps resolution
international.headline: UN General Assembly approves equal-area world maps initiative
facts: The United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution promoting equal-area world maps that show the relative land areas of countries and continents more accurately.
Togo introduced the resolution under the “Correct the Map” initiative; 164 of 193 UN member states supported it, including India, while the United States voted against it.
Equal-area maps preserve relative area but may distort shapes, angles or distances; the resolution concerns visual representation and does not change borders, territories or sovereignty.
The Mercator Projection, developed by Gerardus Mercator in 1569, is useful for marine navigation because constant compass bearings appear as straight lines.
On a Mercator map, high-latitude regions appear larger than their actual size; Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland.
international.summary: The UN General Assembly supported the use of equal-area maps to better represent relative land size. India supported the resolution, introduced by Togo, while the United States voted against it.
international.staticLink: Map projections: equal-area projections and the Mercator Projection.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The resolution was supported by 164 of 193 UN members, including India; the Mercator Projection dates to 1569.
international.mainsAngle: Discuss how map projections shape perceptions of global geography and the trade-offs among preserving area, shape, distance and direction.

international.canonicalTopic: Kathmandu Declaration on illegal wildlife trade
international.headline: SAWEN members adopt Kathmandu Declaration against illegal wildlife trade
facts: Members of the South Asia Wildlife Enforcement Network (SAWEN) unanimously adopted the Kathmandu Declaration at the network’s first General Assembly in Kathmandu, Nepal.
The declaration calls for regional cooperation to prevent, detect and suppress illegal wildlife trade and related transnational organised crime.
It identifies links between wildlife trafficking, corruption, illicit financial flows, other serious crimes, digital-technology misuse and vulnerabilities at international borders.

international.canonicalTopic: India-France TRISHNA Earth observation mission
international.headline: India-France TRISHNA mission scheduled for launch aboard PSLV
facts: TRISHNA, short for Thermal InfraRed Imaging Satellite for High-resolution Natural resource Assessment, is being jointly developed by ISRO and France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES).
The mission is scheduled to launch aboard the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle next year, as stated in the notes.
It is designed to observe land-surface temperature, emissivity and biophysical-radiative variables at high spatial and temporal resolution.

Planned applications include monitoring land energy and water balance, water stress, water quality, urban heat islands, volcanic thermal anomalies, geothermal resources, snowmelt runoff and glacier dynamics.
The mission is also expected to provide information on Aerosol Optical Depth, atmospheric water vapour and cloud cover.

international.canonicalTopic: India-France private-space agreements
international.headline: Indian and French space companies sign three cooperation agreements
facts: Three agreements between Indian and French private space companies were reported to strengthen bilateral space cooperation.

Dhruva Space and Safran signed agreements worth more than €5 million, approximately ₹55 crore, covering communication systems, inertial navigation units, optical payloads and ground stations for India’s SBS-3 space-surveillance satellite constellation.
The notes state that 52 SBS-3 satellites are planned for launch during 2027–30; Safran had earlier participated in Chandrayaan-3.

AXISCADES and U-Space signed a commercial cooperation agreement addressing commercial and institutional requirements in India’s microsatellite market.
The agreements followed an understanding during French President Emmanuel Macron’s India visit in February 2026 on civilian satellites and human spaceflight programmes.

international.headline: Researchers visualise how negatively charged DNA strands bind
facts: Researchers from the Universities of Sheffield and York in the United Kingdom used high-performance Atomic Force Microscopy to visualise how two negatively charged DNA double strands bind.

international.canonicalTopic: Forests for Food: Nourishing People, Sustaining the Planet
international.headline: FAO and Landscape Alliance report examines forests and food security
facts: The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and Landscape Alliance jointly released “Forests for Food: Nourishing People, Sustaining the Planet” through the Collaborative Partnership on Forests initiative.
The report examines forests’ relationship to food security and nutrition, including availability, access, utilisation and stability.
It states that more than 5 billion people depend to some extent on forests for livelihoods, while more than 50,000 wild species are used for food, energy, medicines and other purposes.
At least 10,000 wild species are directly consumed as food; in remote forest communities, wild foods can provide up to 80% of daily protein.
In 2022, around 1.8 billion people, or 23% of the global population, primarily relied on wood fuel for cooking; 410 million used it to boil and purify drinking water.
Forests support pollinators contributing to 35% of global crop production, and forested watersheds supply freshwater to more than 85% of the world’s major cities.

The report says that around 10.9 million hectares of forests were lost annually during 2015–25; annual net forest loss fell from 10.7 million hectares in 1990–2000 to 4.12 million hectares in 2015–25.
international.summary: The report highlights forests’ contribution to food, livelihoods, water, energy and health, while drawing attention to forest loss and gaps in policy coordination and consumption data.
international.prelimsTakeaway: The report was jointly released by FAO and Landscape Alliance under the Collaborative Partnership on Forests initiative.
international.mainsAngle: Integrating forestry, agriculture and health policy is important for food security, rural livelihoods and ecosystem protection.

international.canonicalTopic: 7th Status of Coral Reefs of the World report
international.headline: Global coral reefs face escalating heat stress, GCRMN report finds
facts: The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network released the 7th Status of Coral Reefs of the World report.
Average global hard coral cover was 9.5% below the 1980–2009 baseline; the report says the decline accelerated particularly after 2010.
Hard coral cover fell by 8.9% during 2023–24, described in the notes as the largest annual relative decline recorded so far.
In 2024, about 87% of monitored reefs experienced anomalous heat stress and 42.6% experienced heat levels associated with severe mortality risk.
During 2019–25, more than 25% of the world’s coral reef area experienced heat stress exceeding 4°C-weeks on four or more occasions.
Major mass-bleaching events were recorded in 1998–99, 2010–11, 2016–17 and 2023–25.
Indian coral reef regions listed in the notes are the Gulf of Kutch, Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Malvan Coast.

international.canonicalTopic: UNEP–CCAC air-pollution report
international.headline: Report estimates millions of premature deaths from air pollution in 2025
facts: A report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) estimated 8.4 million premature deaths from air pollution in 2025.
The estimate included 6.4 million deaths from outdoor air pollution linked to PM2.5 and ozone and 2 million from household air pollution; around 300,000 deaths were among children.
The report associated air pollution with 5.5 million new childhood asthma cases and around 2 million new dementia cases in 2025.
It recommended 25 measures across industry, energy, transport, agriculture, households and waste management.
Full implementation of the measures could prevent 144 million premature deaths by 2050 and generate economic benefits equivalent to around 4.5% of global GDP.

international.prelimsTakeaway: The report was prepared by UNEP and CCAC; its proposed measures span six sectors.
international.mainsAngle: Coordinated action on air pollution and climate pollutants can yield public-health and economic gains.

national.canonicalTopic: Appointments to National Commission for Safai Karamcharis
national.headline: Bhagwat Prasad Makwana appointed NCSK Chairman
facts: The Union Government appointed Bhagwat Prasad Makwana of Uttarakhand as Chairman of the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK).

The NCSK monitors sanitation workers’ working conditions and welfare and the implementation of related welfare programmes.

The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 prohibits manual scavenging and provides for rehabilitation; Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
The NAMASTE programme promotes safety, dignity and mechanisation in sanitation work.

national.canonicalTopic: Supreme Court proceedings concerning Vande Mataram
national.headline: Supreme Court considers challenge over singing all stanzas of Vande Mataram
facts: The Supreme Court observed that criminal action should not be taken against a person who declines, on religious grounds, to sing all six stanzas of Vande Mataram.

The three-judge Bench comprised Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohan; it directed the Centre to respond within two weeks to a petition by Carnatic musician T.M. Krishna.

The petition challenged the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026, which received Presidential assent on August 6, 2026, and extended legal protection to the National Song Vande Mataram.
The notes state that intentionally preventing the National Song from being sung or disturbing an assembly engaged in singing it may attract imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both.

The petitioner also challenged February 2026 Ministry of Home Affairs directions requiring all six stanzas at government and official cultural programmes; the notes say the first two stanzas were traditionally commonly sung.

The Court said it would consider the issue in light of Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), which protected students who respectfully stood for the National Anthem but did not sing for genuine religious reasons.
Vande Mataram was written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay for Anandamath and was first sung by Rabindranath Tagore at the 1896 Calcutta Session of the Indian National Congress.
national.summary: The Supreme Court began considering whether a person may decline to sing all six stanzas of Vande Mataram on religious grounds, with reference to the Bijoe Emmanuel ruling.
national.staticLink: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) concerned Articles 19(1)(a) and 25 and freedom of expression and conscience.
national.prelimsTakeaway: The case was before a Bench of Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohan; the Court asked the Centre to respond within two weeks.
national.mainsAngle: The proceedings raise questions about the balance between national symbols, statutory protection and constitutional freedoms of conscience and expression.

national.canonicalTopic: Written communication of grounds of arrest under Article 22(1)
national.headline: Supreme Court clarifies requirement to provide written grounds of arrest
facts: The Supreme Court clarified that an arrested person must receive the grounds of arrest in writing and in a language they understand; Article 22(1) applies regardless of the offence’s nature or seriousness.
The safeguard applies to ordinary offences and arrests under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
Written grounds should ordinarily be supplied at arrest; where that is not possible, they may first be conveyed orally but must later be given in writing within a reasonable time.
Written grounds must be provided at least two hours before production before a Magistrate for remand; non-compliance makes the arrest and subsequent remand illegal.

For re-arrest after release due to an Article 22(1) violation, written grounds and permission from the concerned Judicial Magistrate are required; the application must explain the earlier failure and obtain approval from the original arresting officer’s immediate superior.
The Court directed departmental disciplinary action against the officer responsible for the violation.

Article 22(1) protects the right to be informed of grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner; Section 47 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita also requires information about grounds of arrest and the right to bail.
national.summary: The Supreme Court set out safeguards for communicating arrest grounds, including written notice in a language understood by the arrested person and a deadline before remand.
national.staticLink: Article 22(1) protects people against arbitrary arrest and detention; Section 47 of the BNSS addresses information about grounds of arrest and bail rights.
national.prelimsTakeaway: Written grounds must ordinarily be given at arrest and, in all circumstances, at least two hours before production for remand.
national.mainsAngle: The ruling underscores procedural safeguards, access to legal representation and accountability in the exercise of arrest powers.

national.canonicalTopic: Retirement age of District Judges in seven States
national.headline: Supreme Court directs seven States to raise District Judges’ retirement age to 62
facts: In All India Judges Association v. Union of India, the Supreme Court directed seven States that had agreed to raise District Judges’ retirement age from 60 to 62 to amend their judicial service rules.
The States are Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal.
A judicial officer who reaches 60 may continue until 62, subject to the concerned High Court assessing eligibility and performance.
Eligible judicial officers who have already passed 60 are not to retire before 62 while the relevant rule amendments are pending.
Articles 233–237 address the subordinate judiciary; Article 235 provides for the High Court’s control over district and subordinate courts.

facts: A study for 2024 by V.K. Patel of Cranfield University, UK, and P.A. Taksal of IIT Kharagpur estimated India’s contribution to global warming at approximately 0.05°C.

national.canonicalTopic: Tso Kar Lake restoration project
national.headline: Ladakh launches restoration project for shrinking Tso Kar Lake
facts: The Ladakh administration launched a project to restore the shrinking Tso Kar Lake and its high-altitude wetland ecosystem.
Tso Kar lies on the Rupshu Plateau in southeastern Ladakh and is a saline lake-wetland complex; “Tso Kar” means “White Lake” in the local Tibetan language.
The Tso Kar Wetland Complex was designated a Ramsar Site in 2020 and comprises Tso Kar and Startsapuk Tso.
The wetland is a habitat for migratory birds, particularly the Black-necked Crane.

national.canonicalTopic: Mission Rangeen Machhli–2031 strategic action plan
national.headline: Vice-President releases ornamental fisheries action plan at Agatti
facts: The Vice-President released the strategic action plan for Mission Rangeen Machhli–2031 at Agatti, Lakshadweep.
The Department of Fisheries under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying is implementing the mission for ornamental fish breeding, rearing and trade.
The plan provides for standards covering breeding, hatcheries, disease control, live-fish transport, quarantine, health surveillance and biosecurity.
Traceability and certification are intended to identify captive-bred fish and discourage illegal collection of endangered coral-reef species.
The mission is linked with PMMSY and envisages specialised production, processing, air-cargo and market clusters.
Coastal fishers, youth and women’s Self-Help Groups are to receive training in ornamental fish farming and reef-compatible aquaculture.

national.canonicalTopic: MatsyaMetri fish-measurement app
national.headline: CMFRI develops an AR app for contact-free fish measurement
facts: The Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI) developed the MatsyaMetri smartphone app to measure fish length and width without physical contact.
The app uses augmented reality through the camera on ARCore-supported Android devices and displays a measurement guide.
It can generate fish length-frequency datasets and export information in CSV format.
The app is intended for fisheries researchers and field survey teams, including work at crowded fish landing centres.
CMFRI was established in 1947 and is headquartered in Kochi, Kerala; it is part of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research.

national.canonicalTopic: Emerging Science Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026
national.headline: Second ESTIC conclave scheduled for New Delhi
facts: The second Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC 2026) is scheduled at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, for October 27–29, 2026; Prime Minister Narendra Modi is to inaugurate it.
The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) is coordinating the three-day conclave, which will involve 13 Ministries.
The theme is “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.”
The programme is to cover 12 emerging technology areas, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, robotics, quantum communication, space technology and agricultural technology.
Its stated objective is to help translate scientific research into market-ready technologies and businesses.
The notes state that the ITPO portal lists October 26–28, 2026, while Central Government and CSIR announcements specify October 27–29, 2026.
CSIR was established in 1942 and is headquartered in New Delhi; its Director General is Dr. N. Kalaiselvi.
national.summary: ESTIC 2026 is scheduled to bring government and science stakeholders together to focus on emerging technologies and pathways from research to market.
national.staticLink: CSIR is an autonomous research and development organisation under the Ministry of Science and Technology.

national.canonicalTopic: Platform for Aggregating Clean Transport
national.headline: PACT platform launched to support zero-emission freight transport
facts: NITI Aayog Member Rajiv Gauba launched the Platform for Aggregating Clean Transport (PACT) at the 5th e-FAST India Summit 2026 in New Delhi.
PACT is intended to bring together transport requirements from shippers, logistics service providers and other stakeholders and turn them into deployment opportunities for clean transport vehicles.
It aims to aggregate demand for zero-emission vehicles on major freight corridors to support deployment at scale, vehicle utilisation and investment sustainability.
The platform is intended to support lower-emission freight transport, clean mobility and sustainable logistics.
e-FAST India stands for Electric Freight Accelerator for Sustainable Transport and is a NITI Aayog initiative.
national.summary: PACT was launched as a demand-aggregation platform intended to help scale zero-emission freight vehicles across India.
national.staticLink: A zero-emission vehicle produces no direct tailpipe emissions during operation; examples in the notes include battery electric and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles.

national.canonicalTopic: Gollalagudi Temple protected as Monument of National Importance
national.headline: Gollalagudi Temple in Telangana receives national monument status
facts: The Union Ministry of Culture issued a final notification declaring Gollalagudi Temple, near Ramappa Temple at Palampet village in Mulugu district, Telangana, a Monument of National Importance.
The protected area covers around 0.25 acres in Survey No. 417/3 near the Ramappa Temple UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Archaeological Survey of India had issued a draft notification on March 6 and invited objections and suggestions before the final notification.
The designation gives the temple and its historical surroundings legal protection, with development activity in the surrounding area subject to regulation.
national.summary: A final Union notification placed the Telangana temple under national-monument protection after an earlier draft notification and public-objection process.
national.staticLink: The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 provides for legal protection of monuments of national importance.

national.canonicalTopic: ASUSE district data for Telangana
national.headline: Rangareddy leads Telangana in unincorporated enterprises and employment
facts: ASUSE district-level data place Rangareddy first in Telangana with 6.92 lakh unincorporated enterprises and 16.89 lakh workers.
Among the reported districts, Nizamabad had 2.52 lakh enterprises and Jagtial 2.04 lakh.
Nirmal had the highest women-owned enterprise share at 79.95%, while Khammam had the lowest at 15.88%.
Women accounted for the highest share of workers in Nizamabad at 69.59% and the lowest in Rangareddy at 20.48%.
Average annual wage per worker was highest in Rangareddy at ₹2,13,195 and lowest in Peddapalli at ₹1,06,328.

ASUSE is conducted by the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation and covers unincorporated non-agricultural enterprises in manufacturing, trade and other services.

facts: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) announced that Dhamra Port in Odisha now operates entirely on renewable electricity.

national.canonicalTopic: Geological Museum project at Bhedaghat–Lamhetaghat
national.headline: Geological Museum planned for Bhedaghat–Lamhetaghat
facts: A geological museum and interpretation centre is planned at Bhedaghat–Lamhetaghat in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, at a stated cost of ₹87 crore.
The Madhya Pradesh Tourism Board is to implement the project across approximately 12 hectares under Swadesh Darshan 2.0.
The planned facility includes six galleries and more than 130 exhibits on Earth’s origin and the geological history of the Narmada Valley and Madhya Pradesh.

facts: Agnikavach Safety Solutions Private Limited launched Agni Kavach as an AI-based industrial safety platform described in the notes as indigenously developed.

national.canonicalTopic: Astrogate Labs optical inter-satellite link terminal

facts: Indian deep-tech startup Astrogate Labs developed an indigenous Optical Inter-Satellite Link terminal for laser communication between satellites.
The terminal is intended to transmit data directly between satellites, including across Low Earth Orbit constellations, reducing dependence on ground stations.
Astrogate Labs showcased AstroLink Micro at the 9th Bengaluru Space Expo–2026 at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre.
The notes state that AstroLink Micro is a space-to-ground laser terminal capable of 10 Gbps, while the new inter-satellite terminal is targeted for full spaceflight readiness by 2027.

national.canonicalTopic: HUMSA-2020-NG Mark-2 sonar induction
national.headline: Navy inducts HUMSA-2020-NG Mark-2 sonar for underwater surveillance
facts: The Indian Navy is inducting the indigenous HUMSA-2020-NG Mark-2 sonar to detect and track hostile submarines and ships.
DRDO’s Naval Physical and Oceanographic Laboratory developed the fourth-generation hull-mounted sonar; Bharat Electronics Limited, Bengaluru, is manufacturing it.
The initial plan is to install the system on 16 ships: seven P17A Nilgiri-class ships, three INS Tushil-class ships, four INS Talwar-class ships, INS Rana and INS Brahmaputra.
The sonar supports underwater acoustic detection, localisation and tracking for anti-submarine warfare.

national.staticLink: SONAR means Sound Navigation and Ranging; the notes identify active and passive sonar types.
national.prelimsTakeaway: Developer: DRDO’s NPOL, Kochi; manufacturer: BEL, Bengaluru; planned initial installation: 16 ships.
national.mainsAngle: Indigenous sensor systems contribute to maritime domain awareness and anti-submarine warfare capability.

national.canonicalTopic: Defence Acquisition Council procurement approvals
national.headline: Defence Acquisition Council gives initial approval to procurement proposals worth ₹1.10 lakh crore
facts: The Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, gave initial approval to proposals worth around ₹1.10 lakh crore for the three Armed Forces.
Around 98% of the proposal value is stated to be sourced from the domestic defence industry.
Army proposals included CBRN reconnaissance vehicles, High Mobility Vehicles, automated mine-laying systems, Advanced Light Helicopters, trawl tanks and Sarvatra bridge systems.
Navy proposals included Arudhra radars and marine gas turbines; proposals were also approved for Air Force fighter aircraft, transport aircraft and helicopters.
national.summary: The council’s initial approvals cover equipment for all three services, with the notes stating that most of the value is proposed to come from domestic industry.
national.staticLink: The Defence Acquisition Council was established in 2001 as part of post-Kargil national security reforms and is chaired by the Union Defence Minister.
national.prelimsTakeaway: Approval value: around ₹1.10 lakh crore; proposed domestic sourcing: around 98%; status: initial approval, not completed procurement.
national.mainsAngle: Procurement decisions involve balancing military readiness, domestic industrial capacity and the stages between approval and delivery.

national.canonicalTopic: Recombinant antivenom for three cobra species

facts: Researchers from the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and the Technical University of Denmark developed a recombinant antivenom targeting venom from the Spectacled Cobra, Monocled Cobra and King Cobra found in India.
The laboratory-produced antivenom uses selected antibodies; the study used antibodies obtained from camelid animals such as llamas.

national.canonicalTopic: Supreme Court-appointed National Task Force study on higher-education student wellbeing

national.canonicalTopic: ADR report on elected representatives changing parties 2022–2026
national.headline: ADR report counts 111 elected representatives who changed parties after election victories
facts: ADR and National Election Watch reported that 111 sitting elected representatives across 17 States and Union Territories changed parties after winning elections during 2022–2026: 26 Lok Sabha MPs, 7 Rajya Sabha MPs and 78 MLAs.

The notes list 32 cases in Nagaland, 20 in West Bengal and 9 in Telangana; ADR cautioned that its list might not be exhaustive because systematically maintained official data were not readily available.

ADR proposed transferring decisions on defection-related disqualification from the Speaker or Chairman to the President at Union level and the Governor at State level, acting on Election Commission advice.
ADR also proposed restrictions on defectors holding ministerial, nominated or other government posts until the next general election.
The anti-defection provisions are in the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985; the current deciding authority is the Speaker or Chairman of the House.
national.summary: The report counted post-election party changes and put forward proposed changes to the process for deciding disqualification and restrictions on defectors.

national.canonicalTopic: Second-hand smoke exposure and deaths in India
national.headline: Study reports rising second-hand-smoke deaths in India
facts: A global analysis published in The Lancet Public Health estimated that deaths attributable to second-hand smoke in India rose from 217,700 in 1990 to 325,600 in 2023, an increase of nearly 50%.
India’s population exposed to second-hand smoke rose from 375 million in 1990 to 444 million in 2023; children made up more than 12% of those exposed.
The 204-country study estimated that 2.71 billion people, or 33.9% of the global population, were exposed in 2023, including 767 million children aged 0–14.
The notes identify the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), 2003, as India’s principal tobacco-control law; Section 4 prohibits smoking in public places.
The National Tobacco Control Programme is implemented by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
national.summary: The study highlights the scale of second-hand smoke exposure in India and worldwide, particularly among children, alongside the health burden associated with exposure.
national.prelimsTakeaway: Section 4 of COTPA, 2003 prohibits smoking in public places; India ratified the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in 2004.
national.mainsAngle: Effective tobacco control requires enforcement of smoke-free public spaces and protection of children and other exposed groups.

national.canonicalTopic: All India Survey on Higher Education decade review
national.headline: AISHE-based review records expansion in higher education
facts: The Ministry of Education released a review of higher-education progress from 2014–15 to 2023–24 based on All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) data.
Between the compared years, universities increased from 760 to 1,289 and colleges from 38,498 to 48,246.
Total higher-education enrolment rose from 3.42 crore to 4.50 crore; the Gross Enrolment Ratio increased from 23.7% to 30%.
PhD enrolment rose from 1.17 lakh to 3.43 lakh; female enrolment reached 2.24 crore and female GER was 31.2%, against 28.9% for males.
The Gender Parity Index increased from 0.92 to 1.08; Scheduled Caste GER rose from 18.9% to 27.8% and Scheduled Tribe GER from 13.5% to 22.8%.
STEM enrolment reached 1.02 crore, and the number of foreign students was 58,134.
NEP 2020 sets a higher-education GER target of 50% by 2035.
national.summary: The AISHE-based review reports growth in institutions and enrolment, alongside improved female and socially disadvantaged group participation.
national.prelimsTakeaway: AISHE collects comprehensive statistics on higher education; GER is enrolment relative to the corresponding 18–23 age-group population.
national.mainsAngle: Expansion of higher education needs to be accompanied by equitable access, quality and progress toward the NEP 2020 GER target.

national.canonicalTopic: WMO State of Global Water Resources 2025

facts: The World Meteorological Organization’s State of Global Water Resources 2025 report said groundwater depletion continued during 2022–25, particularly in north-western India, mainly because of excessive extraction.
Monitoring stations reporting below-normal to extremely low groundwater levels rose from 25% in 2024 to 34% in 2025.
The report said terrestrial water storage was below normal in several regions in 2025, including northern India.

facts: India aims to eliminate hepatitis B and C as public-health threats by 2030 through the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme.

facts: Jharkhand’s Mandar folk percussion instrument received Geographical Indication recognition from the Geographical Indications Registry in Chennai.

national.canonicalTopic: Haryana Parali Protection Force
national.headline: Haryana announces a force to curb stubble burning
facts: Haryana announced a special ‘Parali Protection Force’ ahead of the paddy harvesting season to prevent crop-residue burning.
The proposed approach includes field surveillance, drone monitoring and midnight patrols at district and block levels.
Farmers are to be encouraged to use Happy Seeder, Super Seeder, mulching, composting and biomass utilisation, with machinery and financial incentives.
Crop-residue burning releases pollutants including PM2.5, PM10 and carbon monoxide.

national.canonicalTopic: Abolition of Digital Communications Commission
national.headline: Central Government abolishes the Digital Communications Commission
facts: The Central Government abolished the Digital Communications Commission, formerly the Telecom Commission, established in 1989 and renamed in 2018.
The commission had served as the telecom sector’s highest decision-making body for 37 years and examined major telecom projects valued between ₹500 crore and ₹1,000 crore.
Such proposals will now go directly to the Expenditure Finance Committee under the Ministry of Finance.
The Telecom Secretary’s approval limit remains ₹100 crore, while the Telecom Minister’s limit remains ₹500 crore.
national.summary: The abolition changes the route for consideration of major telecom proposals, which are to go directly to the Expenditure Finance Committee.
national.prelimsTakeaway: The DCC was established in 1989, renamed in 2018 and abolished by the Central Government; major proposals are redirected to the Expenditure Finance Committee.
national.mainsAngle: Consider how changes to administrative decision-making structures can affect appraisal and approval of public expenditure and infrastructure proposals.

andhraPradesh.canonicalTopic: ASI proposed protection for five Andhra Pradesh heritage sites
andhraPradesh.headline: ASI proposes protected status for five historical sites in Andhra Pradesh
facts: The Archaeological Survey of India issued draft notifications proposing protected status for five historical and archaeological sites in Andhra Pradesh.

The proposed sites are Konda Reddy Buruju in Kurnool; Lingalakonda and Bojjannakonda at Sankaram in Anakapalli district; Salihundam in Srikakulam district; and Nagarjunakonda Buddhist monuments at Pullareddygudem (Agraharam) in Palnadu district.
The proposal would bring the sites under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Rules, 1959.
The stated purpose is to restrict mining, blasting and other hazardous activities around the sites and regulate construction and repair activities.
Bojjannakonda and Lingalakonda are Buddhist heritage sites associated with ancient monasteries and rock-cut architectural traditions.

The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act was enacted in 1958; the notes describe an ancient monument as generally having at least 100 years of existence and historical, archaeological or artistic significance.

facts: The Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) is conducted by the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
ASUSE covers unincorporated non-agricultural enterprises in manufacturing, trade and other services, measuring their size, employment and economic characteristics.
Kakinada recorded the highest average monthly wage per worker at ₹16,648.58 (₹1,99,783 annually); Kurnool recorded the lowest at ₹9,295.75 (₹1,11,549 annually).

Nandyal had the highest share of women-owned enterprises at 35.89% and women workers at 43.38%; Parvathipuram Manyam had the lowest women-owned enterprise share at 19.38%, and YSR Kadapa the lowest women-worker share at 30.68%.
Officially registered enterprises accounted for 56.60% in Nandyal, the highest district share, and 19% in West Godavari, the lowest.

andhraPradesh.canonicalTopic: State-Level Steering Committee for tiger conservation in NSTR
andhraPradesh.headline: Andhra Pradesh constitutes tiger-conservation committee for NSTR
facts: The Andhra Pradesh Government constituted a State-Level Steering Committee for tiger conservation and inter-departmental coordination in Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR).
Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu is the committee’s Chairman and Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan its Vice-Chairman.
The committee was set up under Section 38U of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

Its membership includes officials from Forest, Tribal Welfare, Panchayat Raj and Rural Development, and Social Welfare departments, as well as wildlife experts, tribal council representatives and the Project Tiger Field Director, Nandyal.
NSTR spans Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in the Nallamala Hills and is associated with the Krishna River.

andhraPradesh.canonicalTopic: Andhra Pradesh Human Organ Transplantation Amendment Act, 2026
andhraPradesh.headline: Governor approves Andhra Pradesh organ-transplantation amendment
facts: The Governor approved the amendment passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature; the Law Department notified it as Andhra Pradesh Act No. 25 of 2026.
The amendment expands the law to cover tissue transplantation, including skin, cornea, heart valves, muscles and bone marrow.
Grandparents and grandchildren were added to the near-relative donor category.
It recognises swap transplantation between two families when the respective donor-recipient pairs are medically incompatible.
The notes state that the amendment followed Supreme Court directions and Jeevandan Board proposals and aims to improve transparency and curb illegal trafficking.
andhraPradesh.summary: The amendment broadens the state’s transplantation framework to include tissues, additional near relatives and legally recognised swap transplants.

andhraPradesh.headline: Andhra Pradesh approves solar, wind-hybrid and compressed-biogas projects
facts: The Andhra Pradesh Energy Department approved renewable-energy projects, with construction required to begin within 10 months and power generation to start within 24 months of approval.
M. Venkata Rao Infra Projects Private Limited received approval for a 675 MW solar project at Madakasira in Sri Sathya Sai district.
Clean Renewable Energy Hybrid-6 Private Limited received approval for a 118.80 MW solar project at Kasanur and Balapanur in YSR Kadapa district.
Sai Bioenergy Andhra Pradesh Private Limited received approval for a 24-tonne-per-day compressed biogas plant in Midthur Mandal, Nandyal district.
Risalven Two Energy Private Limited received approval for a 100 MW wind-solar hybrid project in Yemmiganur Mandal, Kurnool district.
The notes state that earlier approval for Megha Engineering and Infrastructures Limited’s 2,000 MW pumped hydro storage project at Kommuru in Annamayya district was cancelled.
Incentives are to be provided under the AP Clean Energy Policy, with APTRANSCO and NREDCAP directed to take necessary measures.

andhraPradesh.canonicalTopic: Drought-resistant rice using foxtail millet gene
andhraPradesh.headline: University of Hyderabad researchers develop drought-resistant rice varieties using foxtail millet gene
facts: Plant Sciences researchers at the University of Hyderabad introduced a foxtail millet gene into rice varieties to develop rice able to withstand severe drought conditions, including conditions associated with El Niño.
The project, led by University Millet Lab founder Dr. M. Muthamilarasan, received ₹80 lakh in Central Government financial assistance.
The gene was introduced into Pusa Basmati, Sona Masuri and IR-64 rice varieties, with positive results reported in the notes.
The developed varieties are to be distributed free to farmers in selected districts of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu for field-level evaluation.
Foxtail millet’s scientific name is Setaria italica.

andhraPradesh.staticLink: The University of Hyderabad is a Central University located in Hyderabad, Telangana.
andhraPradesh.prelimsTakeaway: The varieties named are Pusa Basmati, Sona Masuri and IR-64; the source gene is from foxtail millet.
andhraPradesh.mainsAngle: Drought-tolerant crops can strengthen climate resilience in agriculture; field evaluation and farmer access are important for assessing their practical value.

mcqs.question: Who was appointed Chairman of the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis?
mcqs.explanation: The Union Government appointed Bhagwat Prasad Makwana as NCSK Chairman, with tenure until March 31, 2028.

mcqs.question: Which organisation’s Travel and Tourism Development Index placed India 31st?
mcqs.explanation: The World Economic Forum developed the index with Zurich Insurance Group; India improved nine places to 31st.

mcqs.question: Which Andhra Pradesh district had the highest number of unincorporated enterprises in the cited ASUSE district data?
mcqs.explanation: Prakasam ranked first with 2,13,162 unincorporated enterprises.

mcqs.question:
Consider the following statements about the Andhra Pradesh organ-transplantation amendment:
1. It expands the law to cover tissue transplantation.
2. It recognises swap transplantation between two families when donor-recipient pairs are medically incompatible.
Which of the above is/are correct?
mcqs.explanation: The amendment covers specified tissues, adds grandparents and grandchildren as near relatives, and recognises medically indicated swap transplantation.

mcqs.question: At the first India–Visegrád Group Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, which position did all four Visegrád Group countries support for India?
options: Permanent membership of the United Nations Security Council
Permanent membership of the International Whaling Commission
mcqs.explanation: The Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia backed India’s candidature for permanent UNSC membership.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT correct about Tso Kar?
options: It lies on the Rupshu Plateau in southeastern Ladakh.
The Tso Kar Wetland Complex comprises Tso Kar and Startsapuk Tso.
It is a saline lake-wetland complex designated a Ramsar Site in 2020.
It is identified as a habitat for the Black-necked Crane.
mcqs.explanation: The incorrect statement is that Tso Kar is in southeastern Ladakh? The supplied facts identify it as a saline lake-wetland complex and the complex as Tso Kar and Startsapuk Tso.

mcqs.question:
Match List I with List II.
List I: 1. Eastern rivers under the Indus Waters Treaty  2. Western rivers under the Indus Waters Treaty
List II: a. Indus, Jhelum and Chenab  b. Ravi, Beas and Sutlej
Choose the correct option.
mcqs.explanation: Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej are the eastern rivers; Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab are the western rivers.

mcqs.question: Which two titles did India win at the 2026 Junior Asia Cup hockey tournaments?
mcqs.explanation: India won both tournaments, defeating South Korea in the men’s final and China in the women’s final.

mcqs.question:
Consider the following statements about Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve:
1. Andhra Pradesh constituted a State-Level Steering Committee for tiger conservation and inter-departmental coordination in the reserve.
2. The committee was constituted under Section 38U of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Which of the above is/are correct?
mcqs.explanation: Both statements are correct; the committee includes state officials, wildlife experts, tribal council representatives, and the Project Tiger Field Director, Nandyal.
